title: MATH3310 Note 3: Best approximation property of Fourier series; "good" and "bad" approximation to the Dirac delta
html:
1. Best approximation property of Fourier series

Last time we considered the vector space C([0,2π],C) {C([0,2\pi],\mathbb{C})}C([0,2π],C) (with coefficient in C {\mathbb{C}}C, of course) and equipped it with the Hermite inner product

⟨f,g⟩=∫[0,2π]f(x)g(x)‾dx.\displaystyle \langle f,g\rangle=\int_{[0,2\pi]}f(x)\overline{g(x)}dx.⟨f,g⟩=∫[0,2π]​f(x)g(x)​dx.

The inner product induces a norm ∥f∥=(⟨f,f⟩)1/2 {\|f\|=\left(\langle f,f\rangle\right)^{1/2}}∥f∥=(⟨f,f⟩)1/2. The distance between two functions f,g {f,g}f,g is then ∥f−g∥ {\|f-g\|}∥f−g∥.

Recall that the n {n}n-th Fourier coefficient is obtained by

f^(n)=12π⟨f,einx⟩,\displaystyle \hat{f}(n)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\langle f,e^{inx}\rangle,f^​(n)=2π1​⟨f,einx⟩,

and we showed that the family {einx}n∈Z {\{e^{inx}\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}}{einx}n∈Z​ is orthogonal, meaning that

⟨einx,eimx⟩={2πif n=m0otherwise.\displaystyle \langle e^{inx},e^{imx}\rangle=\begin{cases} 2\pi & \text{if }n=m\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}.⟨einx,eimx⟩={2π0​if n=motherwise​.

In other words, ⟨f,einx∥einx∥⟩einx∥einx∥=f^(n)einx {{\displaystyle \langle f,\frac{e^{inx}}{\|e^{inx}\|}\rangle\frac{e^{inx}}{\|e^{inx}\|}=\hat{f}(n)e^{inx}}}⟨f,∥einx∥einx​⟩∥einx∥einx​=f^​(n)einx is obtained by projecting f {f}f onto the 1-dimensional linear subspace spanned by einx {e^{inx}}einx. And the Fourier series of f {f}f the summation of all these orthogonal pieces together

∑n∈Zf^(n)einx.\displaystyle \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\hat{f}(n)e^{inx}.n∈Z∑​f^​(n)einx.

With this geometric picture in mind we can now prove quite easily that, e.g. the projected function f^(n)einx {\hat{f}(n)e^{inx}}f^​(n)einx minimizes the distance

∥f−g∥,g=ceinx,c∈C.\displaystyle \|f-g\|,\quad g=ce^{inx},c\in\mathbb{C}.∥f−g∥,g=ceinx,c∈C.

This will follow from Pythagoras theorem for inner product spaces.

Theorem 1 (Pythagoras) Let (V,⟨⋅,⋅⟩) {(V,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)}(V,⟨⋅,⋅⟩) be an inner product space. If X,Y∈V {X,Y\in V}X,Y∈V and ⟨X,Y⟩=0 {\langle X,Y\rangle=0}⟨X,Y⟩=0, then

∥X+Y∥2=∥X∥2+∥Y∥2.\displaystyle \|X+Y\|^{2}=\|X\|^{2}+\|Y\|^{2}.∥X+Y∥2=∥X∥2+∥Y∥2.

Proof: Expanding the squre ∥X+Y∥2 {\|X+Y\|^{2}}∥X+Y∥2 and using the bilinearity and symmetric property of the inner prodcut we find that

∥X+Y∥2=⟨X+Y,X+Y⟩=⟨X,X+Y⟩+⟨Y,X+Y⟩=⟨X,X⟩+⟨X,Y⟩+⟨Y,X⟩+⟨Y,Y⟩=∥X∥2+∥Y∥2.\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} \|X+Y\|^{2} & = & \langle X+Y,X+Y\rangle\\ & = & \langle X,X+Y\rangle+\langle Y,X+Y\rangle\\ & = & \langle X,X\rangle+\langle X,Y\rangle+\langle Y,X\rangle+\langle Y,Y\rangle\\ & = & \|X\|^{2}+\|Y\|^{2}. \end{array}∥X+Y∥2​====​⟨X+Y,X+Y⟩⟨X,X+Y⟩+⟨Y,X+Y⟩⟨X,X⟩+⟨X,Y⟩+⟨Y,X⟩+⟨Y,Y⟩∥X∥2+∥Y∥2.​

□ \Box□

Now to show the minimization property, we consider for arbitrary c∈C {c\in\mathbb{C}}c∈C,

∥f−ceinx∥2=∥f−f^(n)einx+(f^(n)−c)einx∥.\displaystyle \|f-ce^{inx}\|^{2}=\|f-\hat{f}(n)e^{inx}+(\hat{f}(n)-c)e^{inx}\|.∥f−ceinx∥2=∥f−f^​(n)einx+(f^​(n)−c)einx∥.

Note that

⟨f−f^(n)einx,einx⟩=⟨f,einx⟩−2πf^(n)=0,\displaystyle \langle f-\hat{f}(n)e^{inx},e^{inx}\rangle=\langle f,e^{inx}\rangle-2\pi\hat{f}(n)=0,⟨f−f^​(n)einx,einx⟩=⟨f,einx⟩−2πf^​(n)=0,

so that f−f^(n)einx {f-\hat{f}(n)e^{inx}}f−f^​(n)einx is orthogonal to (f^(n)−c)einx {(\hat{f}(n)-c)e^{inx}}(f^​(n)−c)einx. Then we have by the Pythagoras theorem,

∥f−ceinx∥2=∥f−f^(n)einx∥2+∥(f^(n)−c)einx∥2.\displaystyle \|f-ce^{inx}\|^{2}=\|f-\hat{f}(n)e^{inx}\|^{2}+\|(\hat{f}(n)-c)e^{inx}\|^{2}.∥f−ceinx∥2=∥f−f^​(n)einx∥2+∥(f^​(n)−c)einx∥2.

Since ∥(f^(n)−c)einx∥2≥0 {\|(\hat{f}(n)-c)e^{inx}\|^{2}\geq0}∥(f^​(n)−c)einx∥2≥0 for any c {c}c, this implies

∥f−f^(n)einx∥2≤∥f−ceinx∥2,∀c∈C.\displaystyle \|f-\hat{f}(n)e^{inx}\|^{2}\leq\|f-ce^{inx}\|^{2},\quad\forall c\in\mathbb{C}.∥f−f^​(n)einx∥2≤∥f−ceinx∥2,∀c∈C.

Exercise 1 Generalise the above argument to any finite sum of the terms in the Fourier series with span{einx} {\text{span}\{e^{inx}\}}span{einx} replaced the corresponding subspace. We thus see that the finite Fourier sum are the best approximation of the given function f {f}f using complex exponentials (i.e. trignometric polynomials), using the norm ∥⋅∥ {\|\cdot\|}∥⋅∥ we defined before as the "error metric''.

Remark 1 The space C([0,2π],C) {C([0,2\pi],\mathbb{C})}C([0,2π],C) is particular nice since we can always make sense of the integrals such as ∫[0,2π]f(x)e−inxdx {\int_{[0,2\pi]}f(x)e^{-inx}dx}∫[0,2π]​f(x)e−inxdx whenever f∈C([0,2π],C) {f\in C([0,2\pi],\mathbb{C})}f∈C([0,2π],C) as a Riemann integral. The above argument will also work for the more general space of Riemann square-integrable functions and Lebesgue square-integrable functions.

We have one more remarkable property of Fourier coefficients, namely

∑n∈Z∣f^(n)∣2=∫[0,2π]∣f(x)∣2dx,f∈C([0,2π],C)\displaystyle \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}|\hat{f}(n)|^{2}=\int_{[0,2\pi]}|f(x)|^{2}dx,\quad f\in C([0,2\pi],\mathbb{C})n∈Z∑​∣f^​(n)∣2=∫[0,2π]​∣f(x)∣2dx,f∈C([0,2π],C)

We call this the isometry property of Fourier coefficient, and the equality is often called the Parseval's identity. This follows from the best approximation property and the Weierstrass approximation theorem, which states that continuous functions can be approximated to arbitrary accuracy by trignometric polynomials. We won't get into the details here. After we introduce the discrete Fourier transform, you will definitely recognize the similarity. Spoiler: discrete Fourier transform is a unitary linear transform of finite dimensional vector space (or unitary up to a constant, depending on the definition convention).

2. Dirichlet kernel; Poisson kernel

The Dirichlet kernel arises from the symmetric partial sum formula

∑∣n∣≤Nf^(n)einθ=∑∣n∣≤N12π∫[0,2π]f(x)e−inxeinθdx=12π∫[0,2π]f(x)∑∣n∣≤Nei(θ−x)ndx=f∗DN(θ)\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} \sum_{|n|\leq N}\hat{f}(n)e^{in\theta} & = & \sum_{|n|\leq N}\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{[0,2\pi]}f(x)e^{-inx}e^{in\theta}dx\\ & = & \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{[0,2\pi]}f(x)\sum_{|n|\leq N}e^{i(\theta-x)n}dx\\ & = & f*D_{N}(\theta) \end{array}∑∣n∣≤N​f^​(n)einθ​===​∑∣n∣≤N​2π1​∫[0,2π]​f(x)e−inxeinθdx2π1​∫[0,2π]​f(x)∑∣n∣≤N​ei(θ−x)ndxf∗DN​(θ)​

where ∗ {*}∗ stands for convolution, and DN(x)=12π∑∣n∣≤Neixn {D_{N}(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{|n|\leq N}e^{ixn}}DN​(x)=2π1​∑∣n∣≤N​eixn is called the n {n}n-th Dirichlet kernel.

Exercise 2 Show that for each N∈N {N\in\mathbb{N}}N∈N,
∫[0,2π]12π∑∣n∣≤Neinxdx=1.\displaystyle \int_{[0,2\pi]}\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{|n|\leq N}e^{inx}dx=1.∫[0,2π]​2π1​∣n∣≤N∑​einxdx=1.

We showed in class that

∑∣n∣≤Neixn=sin⁡(N+12)xsin⁡12x\displaystyle \sum_{|n|\leq N}e^{ixn}=\frac{\sin(N+\frac{1}{2})x}{\sin\frac{1}{2}x}∣n∣≤N∑​eixn=sin21​xsin(N+21​)x​

and below I plotted the graph for this kernel when N=1,4,10 {N=1,4,10}N=1,4,10 respectively.

You can see that the kernel fluctuate more and more when N {N}N gets larger, peaking at origin. Notice also that the it takes both positive and negative values. This type of fluctuatation should be considered as very large. In fact, one can show

∫[0,2π]∣DN(x)∣dx≥Clog⁡N\displaystyle \int_{[0,2\pi]}|D_{N}(x)|dx\geq C\log N∫[0,2π]​∣DN​(x)∣dx≥ClogN

for some constant C>0 {C>0}C>0. This implies that the absolute integral of the Dirichlet kernels cannot be uniformly bounded. It is this fact that leads to the Gibbs phenomenon we mentioned in the last tutorial. Nevertheless, it is possible to make sense of the convergence in appropriate sense

DN(x)→δ0(x)\displaystyle D_{N}(x)\rightarrow\delta_{0}(x)DN​(x)→δ0​(x)

where δ0(x) {\delta_{0}(x)}δ0​(x) is the "Dirac delta function'' at the origin. For example, the pointwise convergence of the symmetric partial sum holds for smooth functions; also, the convergence

∑∣n∣≤Nf^(n)einx→f(x) in the norm ∥⋅∥,\displaystyle \sum_{|n|\leq N}\hat{f}(n)e^{inx}\rightarrow f(x)\text{ in the norm }\|\cdot\|,∣n∣≤N∑​f^​(n)einx→f(x) in the norm ∥⋅∥,

can be seen as

f∗DN→f∗δ0=f in the norm ∥⋅∥.\displaystyle f*D_{N}\rightarrow f*\delta_{0}=f\text{ in the norm }\|\cdot\|.f∗DN​→f∗δ0​=f in the norm ∥⋅∥.

We only need to know the qualitative behavior here. In any case, the Dirichlet kernel can be thought of a "bad'' approximation of the "Dirac delta function''.

Now we turn to the Poisson kernel. It is closely related to the following boundary value problem

{Δu=0in B(0,1)⊂R2u=u0on ∂B(0,1).(1) \displaystyle \begin{cases} \Delta u=0 & \text{in }B(0,1)\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}\\ u=u_{0} & \text{on }\partial B(0,1) \end{cases}. (1){Δu=0u=u0​​in B(0,1)⊂R2on ∂B(0,1)​.(1)

In class we made the ansatz that the solution is of the form

u(r,θ)=a0+∑k=1∞(akcos⁡kθ+bksin⁡kθ)rk\displaystyle u(r,\theta)=a_{0}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(a_{k}\cos k\theta+b_{k}\sin k\theta)r^{k}u(r,θ)=a0​+k=1∑∞​(ak​coskθ+bk​sinkθ)rk

where (r,θ) {(r,\theta)}(r,θ) is the polar coordinate in R2 {\mathbb{R}^{2}}R2. Using Exercise 4 of Tutorial note 2, we can recognize it as the so-called Abel summation of the Fourier series of a real valued function

∑n∈Zr∣n∣g^(n)einθ.\displaystyle \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}r^{|n|}\hat{g}(n)e^{in\theta}.n∈Z∑​r∣n∣g^​(n)einθ.

Note that when 0<r<1 {0<r<1}0<r<1, this expression is absolutely summable if e.g. g^(n) {\hat{g}(n)}g^​(n) are uniformly bounded!
What is the function g {g}g here? Suppose g {g}g, defined on the unit circle ∂B(0,1) {\partial B(0,1)}∂B(0,1), is nice and smooth. Letting r→1 {r\rightarrow1}r→1, we should have

∑n∈Zg^(n)einθ=g(θ)=u0(θ).\displaystyle \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\hat{g}(n)e^{in\theta}=g(\theta)=u_{0}(\theta).n∈Z∑​g^​(n)einθ=g(θ)=u0​(θ).

In other words,

g^(n)=u0^(n).\displaystyle \hat{g}(n)=\widehat{u_{0}}(n).g^​(n)=u0​​(n).

Hence

u(r,θ)=∑n∈Zr∣n∣u0^(n)einθ=∑n∈Zr∣n∣12π∫[0,2π]u0(x)e−inxdx=12π∫[0,2π]u0(x)∑n∈Zr∣n∣ein(θ−x)dx\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} u(r,\theta) & = & \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}r^{|n|}\widehat{u_{0}}(n)e^{in\theta}\\ & = & \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}r^{|n|}\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{[0,2\pi]}u_{0}(x)e^{-inx}dx\\ & = & \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{[0,2\pi]}u_{0}(x)\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}r^{|n|}e^{in(\theta-x)}dx \end{array}u(r,θ)​===​∑n∈Z​r∣n∣u0​​(n)einθ∑n∈Z​r∣n∣2π1​∫[0,2π]​u0​(x)e−inxdx2π1​∫[0,2π]​u0​(x)∑n∈Z​r∣n∣ein(θ−x)dx​

which again we recognize as a convolution

u(r,θ)=u0∗Pr(θ)\displaystyle u(r,\theta)=u_{0}*P_{r}(\theta)u(r,θ)=u0​∗Pr​(θ)

where

Pr(θ)=12π∑n∈Zr∣n∣einθ=12π(re−iθ1−re−iθ+1+reiθ1−reiθ)=12π1−r21+r2−2rcos⁡θ\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} P_{r}(\theta) & = & \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}r^{|n|}e^{in\theta}\\ & = & \frac{1}{2\pi}(\frac{re^{-i\theta}}{1-re^{-i\theta}}+1+\frac{re^{i\theta}}{1-re^{i\theta}})\\ & = &\frac{1}{2\pi} \frac{1-r^{2}}{1+r^{2}-2r\cos\theta} \end{array}Pr​(θ)​===​2π1​∑n∈Z​r∣n∣einθ2π1​(1−re−iθre−iθ​+1+1−reiθreiθ​)2π1​1+r2−2rcosθ1−r2​​

is the Poisson kernel with parameter r {r}r. We can check that the solution to the boundary value problem (1) is given by convolution of the boundary value with the Poisson kernel.

Exercise 3 Show that for all 0<r<1 {0<r<1}0<r<1,
∫[0,2π]∣Pr(θ)∣dθ=1.\displaystyle \int_{[0,2\pi]}|P_{r}(\theta)|d\theta=1.∫[0,2π]​∣Pr​(θ)∣dθ=1.
Note that Pr(θ)>0 {P_{r}(\theta)>0}Pr​(θ)>0 for all 0<r<1 {0<r<1}0<r<1 and θ∈[0,2π] {\theta\in[0,2\pi]}θ∈[0,2π].

Now you should think of u(r,θ) {u(r,\theta)}u(r,θ) as an approximation of u0 {u_{0}}u0​ here, where you have a parameter r {r}r to adjust how closely you want it to approximate u0 {u_{0}}u0​ (by making r {r}r close to 1 {1}1) or how smooth you want u(r,θ) {u(r,\theta)}u(r,θ) (by making r {r}r closer to zero). You can compare r {r}r with the N {N}N in Dirichlet kernel. I plotted the kernel for r=0.3,0.5,0.8 {r=0.3,0.5,0.8}r=0.3,0.5,0.8 below.

Notice that the kernel is always positive and its absolute integral is uniformly bounded. This stands in strong contrast to the Dirichlet kernel. And we say that the Poisson kernal is a "good'' approximation of the "Dirac delta function".

There is also a physical interpretation for the Poisson kernel. Imaging putting a ideal charge on the boundary of the disk, say at (1,0)(1,0)(1,0). Then the Poisson kernel describes the (negative) electrical potential inside the unit disk. I plotted the figure below.
